name: Frostcrown Citadel

relationships.label: Frostcrown Citadel is the seat of Valdenmoor's throne — the king rules from its frozen halls, surrounded by the slow decay of the Ashen Crown's dying court.

Below the citadel's official chambers, in the ancient ice tunnels carved by glacial flow, the Cult of the Broken Moon conducts forbidden rituals — tolerated and secretly funded by the king's own agents.
Vel-Thara's entropic influence seeps through the citadel's foundations — memories fray, stones crack, and the court grows hollow as her decay spreads through the fortress.
Valdenmoor's lords, operating from Frostcrown Citadel, secretly purchase moon fragments from the Tide-Weavers through intermediaries who pass through the citadel's merchant gates.

description: Frostcrown Citadel is the capital of Valdenmoor, a fortress-city carved into the face of a glacier in the northern reaches of Northern Velkaris. Its walls are living ice fused with black stone, its towers wrapped in perpetual frost, its throne room heated only by the bodies of the dying court. The king rules from here, presiding over a kingdom locked in slow entropic decay, while his agents secretly fund moon cults in the ice tunnels beneath the city. Frostcrown is not a thriving capital — it is a waiting room for a kingdom that knows it is dying and cannot decide whether to fight or freeze.
excerpt: The capital of Valdenmoor — a fortress-city carved into a glacier, where a dying king rules over a dying court while secretly funding forbidden moon rituals in the ice tunnels below.
content:
Frostcrown Citadel does not rise from the glacier — it grows out of it, as if the mountain itself decided to form a scar in the shape of a fortress. The walls are not built; they are carved, layers of black stone fused into ancient ice by a technique no living mason remembers. The result is a structure that sweats frost year-round, its towers wrapped in rime so thick that lookouts must chip the ice from arrow slits every morning or the windows seal shut.

The court inside is a theater of slow death. The king sits on a throne of fossilized bone, wrapped in furs that cannot stop the shaking in his hands. His lords whisper in corners, their words stolen by echoes that never quite fade. Meals are served cold because there is no fuel to heat the ovens. Songs are sung in minor keys because no one remembers a major one. The citadel's great hall — once a ballroom — is now a dormitory for refugees who sleep between the pillars and die quietly in the night. The frost has crept into the court's lungs. Everyone coughs. No one heals.

Below the throne, invisible to the court, lies another Frostcrown. Ancient ice tunnels — carved not by hands but by water that predates the kingdom — wind beneath the fortress in a labyrinth no map records. It is here that the king's agents meet the Cult of the Broken Moon, exchanging coin for promises and moon fragments for silence. The tunnels amplify sound in strange ways: a whisper in the cult's chamber can be heard clearly in the king's private study three hundred feet above. He knows everything they say. He pretends he does not. That is the arrangement.

name: The Sunken Quarter

relationships.label: The Sunken Quarter was once the thriving merchant district of Greyvast's capital, now submerged in mist and seawater — a corpse district of the Sunken Throne.
The Tide-Weavers' primary excavation operations are based in the Sunken Quarter — its flooded merchant vaults and collapsed warehouses yield the richest moon fragment hauls.
The Pale Dominion's priest-crews contest the Sunken Quarter with the Tide-Weavers, claiming divine right to its fragments while the Tide-Weavers claim salvage rights.
The Sunken Quarter was destroyed during the Fall of Greyvast — the moon fragment's impact wave and subsequent flooding submerged the district permanently.

description: The Sunken Quarter is what remains of Greyvast's once-bustling merchant district — a drowned necropolis of collapsed warehouses, flooded vaults, and submerged market squares, all wreathed in the same perpetual mist that shrouds the rest of the Sunken Throne. What was once streets are now canals of frigid black water. What was once storefronts are now caves accessible only by rope and nerve. The Tide-Weavers work these waters, pulling moon fragments from silt-choked basements. The Pale Dominion sends priest-crews to claim the same fragments in the name of Yssara. Beneath the silt, beneath the rubble, beneath the water, older things stir — awakened by the fragment's light, disturbed by the excavators' ropes and hooks. The Tide-Weavers know something is down there. They continue digging anyway.
excerpt: The drowned merchant district of Greyvast's capital — a submerged necropolis of flooded vaults and mist-choked streets, contested by the Tide-Weavers and the Pale Dominion, where something older stirs beneath the silt.
content:
The Sunken Quarter was not hit by the moon fragment directly. It drowned from the shockwave. The impact of the Fall of Greyvast cracked the seabed and sent a wall of water racing through the merchant district faster than anyone could run. The water did not recede. It pooled, turned black, and stayed. What was once a market square is now a cistern forty feet deep. The upper floors of the counting houses jut from the surface like broken teeth, their windows dark, their interiors home only to mist and silence.

The Tide-Weavers know this water better than anyone. They navigate it in flat-bottomed skiffs, silent as grave-walkers, their lanterns casting circles of green light that do not reach the bottom. They lower cages and hooks into the flooded vaults below, feeling for fragments with practiced patience. Sometimes they pull up coins stamped with a king's face no one remembers. Sometimes they pull up bones that do not belong to any known creature. The best hauls come from the deepest chambers — merchant vaults sealed for centuries before the Fracture, their contents undisturbed, their locks rusted through, their guardians still waiting.

The Pale Dominion watches from the edges. They do not descend into the water themselves — they consider it beneath their dignity — but their priest-crews patrol the half-submerged streets above, claiming every fragment the Tide-Weavers bring to the surface as divine property of Yssara. Skirmishes break out in the mist. Shots are fired. Bodies sink. The Quarter accepts them the same way it accepts everything: silently, darkly, one layer deeper into the silt. Below the silt, in the bedrock beneath the merchant vaults, there are carvings that predate Greyvast itself. The Tide-Weavers have found them. They have not told the Pale Dominion. They have not told anyone what the carvings say.

description: The Sunken Quarter is the drowned corpse of Greyvast's old merchant district — a partially submerged ruin now serving as the Tide-Weavers' primary excavation site. Before the Fall of Greyvast, this was the richest commercial hub in Northern Velkaris, with vaults stuffed with pre-Fracture coin and warehouses full of goods from across the frozen continent. Now it is a flooded necropolis, its streets turned to canals, its buildings hollowed by impact and tide. The Tide-Weavers work its ruins with ropes and lanterns, hauling moon fragments from depths that grow more dangerous the deeper they descend. The Pale Dominion contests every excavation, and skirmishes between Tide-Runner crews and Dominion priest-soldiers are weekly occurrences in the Quarter's mist-choked streets.
excerpt: The drowned merchant district of Greyvast's capital — now the Tide-Weavers' primary excavation site and a contested battlefield between salvagers and the Pale Dominion.
content:
The Sunken Quarter was once the heart of Greyvast's wealth. Now it is a flooded scar, a district-sized wound in the earth where seawater meets mist and the boundary between street and canal has been erased entirely. The buildings that remain stand at angles that defy gravity, their foundations gutted by the impact wave, their upper floors accessible only by rope and nerve. The Tide-Weavers have mapped seven levels of descent. They have not reached the bottom.

Every morning, Tide-Runner crews lower themselves into the Quarter's depths through holes cut in what were once market square roofs. They work in teams of three: one diver, one rope-handler, one lookout for the Pale Dominion. The mist here is thicker than elsewhere — it swallows sound and distorts depth perception — and the water below is cold enough to stop a heart in minutes. The moon fragments rest in the drowned vaults of old merchant houses, cushioned by silt and the bones of those who stayed to guard their coin.

The Pale Dominion watches from the Quarter's edge. Their priest-crews have attempted three descents in the past year. Each time, the Tide-Weavers cut their ropes. Each time, the Dominion sends more priests. The Quarter does not belong to either side — it belongs to the mist, and the mist tolerates no one for long.

name: Ashenveil

relationships.label: Valdenmoor tolerates Ashenveil's existence as a buffer zone and trading post, though the Ashen Crown's lords despise the lawlessness they permit at their border.
The Oathbound Remnants recruit heavily from Ashenveil's displaced Greyvast refugees, finding eager volunteers among those who lost everything in the Fall.
The Tide-Weavers use Ashenveil's unregulated market as a smuggling hub for moon fragments, evading both Valdenmoor's tariffs and the Pale Dominion's censors.
The Pale Dominion's missionaries and agents push into Ashenveil's outskirts, claiming the souls of the displaced as their divine right — a creeping occupation the town cannot stop.
Ashenveil was founded by refugees fleeing the Fall of Greyvast — a desperate camp that refused to disperse, built from scavenged stone and the bones of a lost kingdom.

description: Ashenveil is a tense, faction-riddled town on the contested borderlands of Northern Velkaris, founded by Greyvast refugees who refused to disperse. It is not a planned settlement — it accreted. A camp became a hamlet, a hamlet became a village, and a village became a town that three factions cannot afford to ignore but none can afford to control. The Oathbound Remnants recruit openly in its streets. The Tide-Weavers trade through its unregulated market. The Pale Dominion's missionaries preach at its gates. Valdenmoor tolerates it as a buffer zone. Every resident is a refugee, every transaction is watched, and everyone knows the truce is temporary.
excerpt: A tense refugee town on the contested borderlands — the Oathbound Remnants recruit here, the Tide-Weavers smuggle here, and the Pale Dominion pushes in from the edges.
content:
Ashenveil began as a camp — refugees from Greyvast who crawled out of the mist and stopped walking. They built walls from the rubble of their former homes, roofs from the sails of wrecked fishing boats, and streets from mud packed so hard by constant traffic that it turned to stone. Twenty years later, no one calls it a camp anymore. It is a town, and it has the desperate permanence of a wound that never heals.

Three factions breathe down Ashenveil's neck. The Oathbound Remnants walk its streets openly, recruiting from the refugee population with promises of reclaimed glory. The Tide-Weavers keep storefronts in the central square, buying and selling moon fragments with no questions asked. The Pale Dominion's priests arrive at the gates every morning and leave every evening, preaching to crowds that shrink a little more each week. Valdenmoor's patrols stop at the town's official border but go no further — the Ashen Crown tolerates Ashenveil because it cannot afford to govern it. The result is a truce held together by mutual distrust. One wrong death, one stolen fragment, one recruit too many, and the town will tear itself apart.

The permanent residents know this. They have built their lives on the fault line, and they accept the risk because nowhere else will have them. The blacksmith forges weapons for the Remnants and tools for the Tide-Weavers in the same fire. The innkeeper takes coin from Pale Dominion priests and Oathbound scouts on the same night. Ashenveil does not survive because it is strong. It survives because every faction needs a place where they can pretend the others do not exist. The day that pretense breaks is the day Ashenveil burns.

name: The Pale Spire

relationships.label: The Pale Spire is the theocratic capital of the Pale Dominion — the Arch-Seers rule from its heights, and all Dominion doctrine originates within its walls.
The Pale Spire is built around the largest known moon fragment, which the Dominion venerates as Yssara's living presence on earth — the city is a temple to her power.
Within the Pale Spire's scriptoriums, the Arch-Seers formalized the First Moon Ritual into sacred doctrine — the Spire is where the ritual became canon.
Heretics of the Cult of the Broken Moon are publicly executed in the Pale Spire's central square — the Dominion considers their interpretation of lunar magic a capital crime.
The moon fragment at the Pale Spire's center radiates a field that slows Vel-Thara's entropic decay — the city is the one place in Northern Velkaris where things do not fall apart.

description: The Pale Spire is the theocratic capital of the Pale Dominion, a vertical city built in concentric rings around the largest moon fragment left by the Celestial Fracture. The fragment — a shard the size of a temple — is embedded in the earth at the city's center, and it glows with a constant, colorless light that casts no shadows and holds the decay of Northern Velkaris at bay. The Arch-Seers rule from the fragment's edge, wearing white robes that never fray, interpreting Yssara's will through the shard's resonant hum. The Spire is the seat of Dominion doctrine, the site where the First Moon Ritual was codified into sacred law, and the place where heretics of the Cult of the Broken Moon are publicly executed. It is the most powerful and the most isolated city in Northern Velkaris — preserved, perfect, and utterly still.
excerpt: The theocratic capital of the Pale Dominion — a vertical city built around the largest moon fragment, where the Arch-Seers rule and heretics are publicly executed beneath a light that never fades.
content:
The Pale Spire does not touch the earth so much as rise from it — a vertical city built in concentric rings around the largest moon fragment the Celestial Fracture left behind. The fragment is the size of a temple, embedded in the ground at the city's absolute center, and it glows with a light that has no source. The glow is constant, colorless, and casts no shadows. At night the Spire is visible from thirty miles away, a pale needle of light stitched into the dark.

The Arch-Seers rule from the fragment's edge. They wear white robes that never stain, never fray, never age — the fragment's field preserves them as it preserves everything within the inner rings. Their voices are soft, their decrees absolute. They do not raise their voices because they do not need to. The city obeys.

In the outer square, where the fragment's protection thins, the executions take place. Heretics of the Cult of the Broken Moon are brought here on the new moon, bound in chains that the fragment's light cannot warm. The sentence is always the same: exposure to the raw, unfiltered energy of the moon shard until the soul erodes. It is not quick. The square is silent during these events. No one screams for long.

The strange thing about the Pale Spire is the stillness. There is no decay. Wood does not rot. Metal does not rust. Bodies do not age. The fragment's field holds entropy at bay within the inner rings, and the result is a city that feels frozen — preserved in amber, perfect and dead. The Arch-Seers call it grace. The rest of Northern Velkaris calls it unnatural. Both are correct.

description: The Pale Spire is the theocratic capital of the Pale Dominion, a tower-city built around the largest moon fragment ever recovered from the Celestial Fracture. The fragment — a shard the size of a temple, embedded in the earth at the city's center — pulses with a constant, colorless light that never dims. The Arch-Seers rule from galleries carved into the fragment's face, interpreting its glow as Yssara's divine will. The city is a monument to controlled power: its streets are geometrically perfect, its white stone walls are immaculate, and its air is still in a way that feels deliberate. The execution square at the fragment's base is never empty. The Pale Spire is not a place of worship. It is a place of certainty.
excerpt: The theocratic capital of the Pale Dominion — a tower-city built around the largest moon fragment, where the Arch-Seers rule, heretics are executed, and decay cannot reach.
content:
The Pale Spire does not glow — it pulses. A light without color, without warmth, without variation, emanating from the moon fragment embedded in the city's heart. The shard is massive, a wedge of pale stone the size of a temple, driven into the earth at an angle that makes it seem both fallen and ascending. The city was built around it, layer upon layer of white stone rising in concentric rings, each tier closer to the fragment than the last. The innermost ring is the Spire itself, the seat of the Arch-Seers, who conduct their rituals on balconies carved directly into the fragment's surface.

The streets of the Pale Spire are silent. Not the silence of emptiness — the city is full of people — but the silence of absolute order. There is no decay here. No frost on the walls, no cracks in the stone, no rot in the wooden beams. The fragment's field suppresses entropy within the city limits. Food does not spoil. Wounds heal cleanly. Memories do not fray. It is a perfection that feels like pressure, and visitors describe the air as heavy, as if the city itself is holding its breath.

At the base of the fragment, in the shadow of the Arch-Seers' galleries, lies the Judgment Square. It is a circle of white stone, unmarked, unadorned. Heretics from the Cult of the Broken Moon are brought here at dawn, bound in chains that have been blessed by three Arch-Seers. The execution is not quick — it is a ritual, prolonged and precise, designed to demonstrate the cost of misinterpretation. The crowd watches in silence. The fragment pulses. The light does not change. The certainty of the Pale Spire is its most oppressive quality: the city has no doubt, and it permits none in those who enter.

name: Mournwall

relationships.label: Mournwall was built and is maintained entirely by the Oathbound Remnants — it is their primary stronghold and the center of their operations against the Pale Dominion.
Mournwall exists as a forward base for the reclamation of Greyvast — every stone in its walls is a promise to return what was lost.
Mournwall is named for Mourne the Hollow King, whose soul-debt binds the Remnants — a city built on oath and grief, dedicated to a god who holds their collective debt.
The Pale Dominion's forces besiege Mournwall's supply lines and launch weekly raids — the city has never fallen, but it has never been safe for a single day.
Mournwall is built on the high ground overlooking the Sunken Quarter — Remnant watchtowers keep constant vigil over the excavation site, monitoring both Tide-Weaver and Dominion movements.

description: Mournwall is a fortress-town built by the Oathbound Remnants on the high ground overlooking Greyvast's sunken ruins. It is half military encampment, half memorial — a city of soldiers who have never known a world before the siege. Every outer wall is carved with the names of the fallen, every watchtower faces the mist of the Sunken Quarter below, and every inhabitant carries the weight of an oath they will die before breaking. Mournwall is not a city that expects to fall — it is a city that expects to fight until there is nothing left to fight with.
excerpt: The Oathbound Remnants' fortress-town on the edge of Greyvast — a city of soldiers, memorial walls, and watchtowers that never rest, built on grief and defiance.
content:
Mournwall is built from the bones of Greyvast. The stone was quarried from the ruined outskirts of the Sunken Throne, carried up the slope by hand, and set in place by survivors who had lost everything else. The walls are thick — thick enough to absorb a siege, thick enough to carve names into. Every Remnant who dies in defense of the city has their name cut into the outer wall before the body is burned. The names face outward, toward the enemy, as if the dead are still holding the line.

The watchtowers never go dark. From Mournwall's highest point, the sentries can see the mist of the Sunken Quarter pooling in the lowlands below, lit from within by the pale glow of Tide-Weaver lanterns and Dominion ritual fires. The Remnants watch the excavation site the way a starving man watches a locked granary — knowing what lies within, knowing they cannot reach it, waiting for a moment that may never come.

The soldiers of Mournwall are young. Most were born after the Fall of Greyvast, raised in the shadow of the oath, trained from childhood to hold a spear and recite the names of the dead. They have never known a world without siege. They eat cold rations on freezing watchtowers, sleep in shifts, and die in numbers that the wall carvers cannot keep up with. The city smells of wet stone and old iron and the particular silence that follows a burial. It is not a happy place. It is not meant to be. It is a promise that has not yet been kept.

description: Mournwall is the Oathbound Remnants' fortress-city and primary stronghold, built on the high ground overlooking the Sunken Quarter and the mist-choked ruins of Greyvast. It is not a city in the traditional sense — it is a wall with a city attached, built entirely for the reclamation of Greyvast and defense against the Pale Dominion. Every stone is engraved with the name of an unrecovered Greyvast citizen. Every structure is defensible. The Remnants maintain Mournwall as both a military base and a memorial, a place where grief is weaponized into purpose. The city has never fallen to Dominion assault, but it has also never known a day of peace.
excerpt: The Oathbound Remnants' fortress-city on the edge of Greyvast — a wall of carved names, a military base, a memorial, and the last defiant outpost against the Pale Dominion.
content:
Mournwall does not have a street. It has a wall — one wall, facing the mist, built from stone hauled out of Greyvast's ruins by hand. The wall is forty feet high and two miles long, and every stone is carved with a name. The names of the dead who have not been recovered. The names of oaths sworn and kept. The names are the city's only decoration. There are no statues, no banners, no monuments. The wall is the monument.

Behind the wall, the city is a functional skeleton. Armories. Mess halls. A temple without a roof — open to the sky, so the dead can see the stars they died under. The Remnants do not build for comfort. They build for readiness. Every structure in Mournwall can be converted to a defensive position in under an hour. Every street is wide enough for a cavalry charge and narrow enough to bottleneck an advancing force. The city is a weapon disguised as a home.

The grief is not hidden. It is the city's atmosphere. The Remnants do not mourn in silence — they mourn in ritual, in song, in the nightly roll call of the unrecovered. Mournwall is named for the Hollow King, but its faith is older than his name: the belief that to be remembered is to be saved, and that to forget is the only true death. Every night, the names on the wall are read aloud. Every night, the mist listens.
